1. Basic Information.Project Title: Workers Don't Go to the Factory
Artist / Group / Collective / Organizer: A group of artists and social activists, with the direct participation of Deh Vanak residents

Location.text: Shahamati Alley, East side of Alzahra University, Deh Vanak, Tehran

sections.title: 2. Short Project Introduction
paragraphs: Workers Don't Go to the Factory is a collective narrative of the history, everyday life, and resistance of the residents of the Deh Vanak neighborhood against official trends of demolition, appropriation, and Gentrification-Induced Displacement.

This project was formed on December 9, 2018, in collaboration with a group of artists, social activists, and neighborhood residents, and was realised in the urban space of the workers' quarter of Deh Vanak.
The event included a collection of photographs, photo-collages, installations, local maps, video art, musical performances using found objects from the demolished houses, and an open tribune.
All these components were created with the direct participation of the neighborhood's people and were exhibited in the Shahamati dead-end alley.

The project sought to collectively represent the lived experience of the residents, the collective memory of the neighborhood, and their resistance against physical and symbolic erasure from the city, directly in the residents' own living space.

sections.title: 3. Context & Site
paragraphs: The project was executed in an urban setting and living context of the Deh Vanak neighborhood, a neighborhood entangled in a long-standing legal land dispute between the residents and Alzahra University.
This dispute began in 2002, with its roots tracing back to the history of the neighborhood's formation.
In 1938, with the establishment of Vanak Factory No. 5, a group of workers settled in company houses around the factory.
Over time, and with the agreement of the factory manager, these workers expanded their homes, and their families remained in this area generation after generation.
After the factory was relocated, the workers and their children remained in the area and considered themselves to have the right of residence.
In the following decades, with the expansion of the city and the establishment of Alzahra University near this area, the conflict over the ownership of lands and houses intensified.
In the summer of 2018, the sudden demolition of several houses by the university was a turning point in this dispute.
The project Workers Don't Go to the Factory took shape in the midst of these tensions and as a cultural and collective reaction to this process.

sections.title: 5. Motivations & Questions
paragraphs: This local exhibition was formed in response to the growing trend of house demolitions in the area, which was a continuation of the same long-standing dispute over the ownership of the workers' houses in this region.

At that time, public attention was mainly focused on the material dimension of land and property, but a group of artists and activists decided to address another aspect of the story: the human, psychological, and identity dimension of this neighborhood and its residents.
The project aimed to depict the lived experience of the inhabitants with a critical yet empathetic look.

For this reason, this project was not merely a documentary of an urban event, but an attempt to revive the collective memory and show the symbolic value of the home as a shelter, memory, and identity.

sections.title: 6. Constraints & Strategies
paragraphs: This project was formed completely independently and without any institutional or official financial support.
Its implementers were a group of artists and social activists who held the exhibition in public space, relying on personal capabilities and the collective solidarity of some residents.
For example, residents provided catering, supplies, and drinks, and the projector and execution equipment were obtained through friendship networks.

The focus of the works was on human narratives, memory, and the lived experience of the residents, and the project tried to convey the narrative without it turning into a slogan or direct political stance.
However, shortly after the start of the exhibition, police and security forces entered the site and tried to stop the continuation of the work; there was pressure to disperse the crowd.

During that same day and afterwards, diverse cultural and social reactions took shape even among different groups of residents: debates about the clothing and behavior of the women present at the event, and even the type of philosophical/political references in the artworks.
According to some residents, immediately after the exhibition, the local people were divided into two different groups.
On the other hand, some activists also joined this event for the interests and strategies of their own group or person.

Furthermore, after the exhibition was held, Alzahra University announced that it intended to file a complaint for trespassing, as it considered the land where the exhibition was held to belong to the university.

sections.title: 11. About the Artist
paragraphs: The project was formed by a group of artists and social activists, with the direct participation of the residents of Deh Vanak
In the project Workers Don't Go to the Factory, the neighborhood residents simultaneously played the roles of audience and creators, and actively participated in various stages of the project.
Their participation included gathering narratives, family photos, and personal items, collaborating in shaping the installations, and attending the open tribune.
Artists and social activists went to the homes of Deh Vanak residents, spoke with them, and explained the idea of the exhibition.
Photos, personal objects, and nostalgic items related to their lives and homes enriched the archival materials for the project.
A part of the artworks took shape from within the ruins and demolished spaces; objects collected from the ruins became raw materials for creating the artwork.

This included musical performances with dishes and remaining objects from the houses, installing photos of residents on the local walls, and holding a collective reading and discussion in the same space.
Visitors directly encountered the installations, photos, and videos by walking through the Shahamati Alley, and they joined a collective experience and face-to-face dialogue with the residents.
Thus, audience interaction took shape in the form of direct participation, conversation, and physical presence in the shared urban space.
In this project, the boundary between the audience and the participant disappeared, and the residents were simultaneously the subject, narrator, and viewer of the work.
